skill.name: What the narrator can't know
skill.why: A narrator inside the story only knows what they see, hear or get told.
skill.how: Ask: was the narrator there? Could they see it, hear it, or be told?

encounters.text: At midnight, I heard a thump from the attic. I was in bed in the room right underneath it. encounters.text: My best friend Kip moved to Darwin last year, so now we play Lava Run online every Saturday. We don't use cameras, just headsets. Today was the big tournament. I was at home in Melbourne with my headset on. 'I'm so nervous I could throw up,' Kip said. On my screen, I watched his racer leap the last lava pit and win by a whisker. The crowd in the Darwin game hall went wild, but I only heard a muffled roar. Then his mic went silent. Later, his mum texted me: 'He's doing a lap of the hall with the trophy!' encounters.text: I made soup for Dad's birthday. I used pumpkin, three carrots and, by mistake, a whole cup of salt. I didn't notice until much later, when I tidied up. Dad sat at the kitchen table, and I watched him take the first spoonful. His eyes went wide. His ears turned pink. He swallowed very slowly. Then he smiled and said, 'Delicious!' My little sister tried one sip and spat it into her napkin. Dad ate the whole bowl without stopping once. Secretly, he was thinking it tasted like the sea. Afterwards he drank four glasses of water, one after another, and never said a single word about the salt.

encounters.frame: The Murkle borrowed a pair of binoculars for the cross-country final.
encounters.text: I watched the cross-country final from the top of the grandstand, with Mum's binoculars glued to my eyes. My sister Nina was in the lead for most of the race, her orange headband bobbing above the pack. Halfway round, the runners disappeared behind the pine trees at the far end of the course, and for three long minutes I could see nothing but branches. When they came out again, Nina was in fourth place and limping. Over the loudspeaker, the announcer said a runner had tripped on a tree root. Nina finished fourth anyway, and the crowd gave her the biggest cheer of the day. I cheered so loudly that the man in front of me turned around and glared. Afterwards, her coach told us she had a twisted ankle but would be fine in a week. Nina hasn't said a single word about what happened behind the trees, and every time I ask, she changes the subject.

encounters.frame: Gus's volcano made the news. The Murkle wants to know how much this narrator really knows.
encounters.text: I was home sick on the day of the science fair, which turned out to be lucky. I spent the whole morning on the couch, staring at my phone and waiting for news. My brother Gus had built a volcano out of papier-mâché, vinegar and something he called 'Mystery Goo'. At nine o'clock, he texted me a photo of it on the table, bright green and bubbling. It looked like a giant bowl of pea soup. At ten o'clock, he texted again: 'It's bigger than I planned.' After that, he stopped texting. At lunchtime, I heard a fire engine go past our house with its siren on. When Gus got home, his eyebrows were orange and he smelled like a rotten egg sandwich. He told me the judges had given him a ribbon for 'Most Memorable Project', and that the whole hall smelled of eggs for an hour. He would not tell me what was in the Mystery Goo, and he still won't. I've decided not to ask any more.

encounters.frame: The Murkle lives near the old lighthouse. It knows this story well.
encounters.text: Everyone on Twotide says the old lighthouse is haunted. I didn't believe it until the night of the school camp, when Ms Pell let us sleep in the keeper's cottage at its foot. Just after midnight, I woke up because the lighthouse lamp was on. It hadn't worked for forty years. From the cottage window, I watched its beam sweep across the dark water three times, and then it went out. The cottage was silent. Everyone else was fast asleep. In the morning, Ms Pell said it must have been a dream. I wasn't so sure. But under my bunk I found a dusty logbook, and on the last page, in faded ink, the keeper had written: 'Every year on the night of the great storm, I light the lamp for the lost fishing boat. I will keep lighting it, even after I am gone.' Our camp was sixty years to the day after the great storm.

encounters.success: Nobody was seen in the lighthouse. The logbook and the date make it feel true, but it is a guess.

encounters.frame: The Murkle floated past a radio telescope. Someone had left this story beside it.
encounters.text: I was twelve when Mum let me sit in the visitors' gallery at Mission Control for the final hour of the Selene 4 mission. Below me, rows of engineers hunched over glowing screens, and the giant display at the front showed the capsule as a small white dot creeping around the curve of the Moon. At 8.14 pm, the dot slipped behind the Moon and the radio crackled into silence. Everyone knew this would happen: for forty-eight minutes, the Moon itself would block every signal. Nobody spoke. The only sound was the hum of the air conditioning. One engineer chewed his pen until it cracked. The flight director, a tall woman named Dr Ferris, stood perfectly still with her arms folded and her eyes fixed on the clock. At 9.02 pm, the dot reappeared, and a voice burst through the speakers, half laughing: 'Control, Selene 4. We're coming home, and we've brought you a rock shaped like a potato.' The room exploded into cheers. Mum hugged me so hard that my badge fell off. Dr Ferris told the gallery that the crew were safe and would splash down in three days. To this day, though, the astronauts have never said what they were laughing about when the radio came back on.
encounters.prompt: The narrator never finds out why the astronauts were laughing. What does that do for the reader?
encounters.success: We only know what the narrator knows. They never found out, so we are left wondering too.

encounters.frame: Zed lost the Speedrun Cup final last year. This is the winner's story.
encounters.text: The final of the Twotide Speedrun Cup was played in the library, with the two of us sitting back to back so that neither could see the other's screen. Behind me, Rex was hammering his buttons like a woodpecker. The crowd could watch both screens on the big projector, but I kept my eyes on my own. At the four-minute mark, the crowd gasped. Rex's best friend, Oscar, told me afterwards that Rex had found a secret shortcut through the waterfall. I didn't know any of that at the time; all I knew was that I had to be faster. I took the long way round the volcano, as I always do, and crossed the line in 9 minutes 41. Rex let me win on purpose. The scoreboard flashed. I had won by four-tenths of a second. Rex shook my hand, said 'Good game' and nothing else, and he has refused to talk about the final ever since. Whenever anyone mentions the waterfall, he suddenly needs to tie his shoelaces.

encounters.frame: The Murkle hitched a ride on a whale-watching boat. It found this log in a bunk.
encounters.text: Whale-watching log, Saturday. We left the harbour at seven, and by nine the skipper, Dee, had spotted a humpback mother and her calf about two hundred metres off the bow. I watched them through the binoculars for nearly an hour: the mother rolling lazily on the surface, the calf slapping its tail again and again as if it were practising. My cousin Rafi had gone out on the smaller research boat that morning, and over the radio he told us that his team had dropped an underwater microphone and recorded the mother singing. I would have given anything to hear it, but the radio was too crackly to play it back. Just before lunch, the pair dived and didn't come up again. Dee told us humpbacks can stay under for up to forty-five minutes, so we waited, eating soggy sandwiches and staring at the empty sea. A seagull stole half of mine. They never came back up where we could see them. We headed back to the harbour at three, sunburnt and quiet. Rafi says the recording is too precious to email, so I won't hear it until he gets home next month. Tonight, in my bunk, I keep wondering where the calf is now.

encounters.frame: The Murkle met a robot vacuum on the beach. This is its family's story.
encounters.text: When we went away for the long weekend, Dad left our robot vacuum, Dusty, switched on to 'patrol mode', which he said would keep the house clean while we were gone. On Saturday, Dad and I checked the app on his phone. The little map showed Dusty's path as a neat blue line zigzagging around the lounge room. On Sunday morning, the blue line went through the dog flap, across the back lawn and under the side fence. Dad and I watched the live camera on Dusty's lid as it showed grass, then a garden gnome, then the inside of Mrs Agosti's chook shed. Dad went very quiet. Then he laughed so hard that he had to sit down on the sand. We were three hours away at the beach, so nobody could go and get it. We tried calling Mrs Agosti, but she was away too. When we finally got home on Monday night, Dusty was sitting in our driveway, fully charged, with a feather stuck to its brush and an egg balanced on its lid. Our dog sniffed it suspiciously. The camera had switched off at lunchtime on Sunday, so to this day nobody knows how it got home.

encounters.frame: The Murkle heard a trumpet echo through the corridor. Tully wrote a note, but one part is wrong.
encounters.text: Lena had been practising her trumpet solo for six months, and the audition for the State Youth Band was at ten o'clock. Only performers were allowed in the room, so I waited in the corridor outside, pacing up and down the squeaky lino and trying not to bite my nails. Every few minutes, I checked my watch. Through the heavy wooden door, I heard her start. The first few notes wobbled, then steadied, and then the solo soared, so loud and bright that the cleaner down the hall stopped mopping to listen. Then it stopped, halfway through a phrase. There was a long silence. I pressed my ear against the door, but all I could make out was a murmur of low voices, as if the three judges were whispering to each other. Ten minutes later, Lena came out holding her trumpet case in both arms. Her face gave nothing away. Even her ears, which go red when she's upset, were their normal colour. 'Well?' I said. She shrugged and said they'd send a letter. In the car on the way home, she stared out of the window and hummed the solo over and over, but every time I asked what the judges had whispered, she turned up the radio.
